candidate.answerReason: Any two students earn at most 24 points together. A score of 13 therefore guarantees a lead; 11 can tie, and 12 cannot be earned.

methods.label: Bound two students' combined score
methods.explanation:
Compare a student with any one rival. In a single race, their combined score is at most \(5+3=8\), since they cannot both win. Across three races, their combined score is therefore at most
\[
3\times8=24.
\]
If one student earns \(13\) points, every rival earns at most \(24-13=11\), so that student must finish ahead of everyone.

To test a lower requirement, two students could score \((5,5,1)\) and \((3,3,5)\) in the three races. Each earns \(11\), so neither earns more than the other. A third student can take the remaining scoring place in each race. This example also defeats every lower point requirement.

A total of \(12\) cannot occur. If a student scores zero in any race, the other two races contribute at most \(10\). Otherwise all three race scores are odd, so their sum is odd.

Finally, \(13\) is attainable with two wins and one second-place finish. The smallest attainable score that guarantees an outright win is therefore \(\boxed{13}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: The proof uses an elementary score bound, a feasible race example, and an odd-even check.

candidate.annotationRationale: Finding the minimum guaranteed score requires a universal bound, a counterexample to lower requirements, and verification that the proposed score is attainable. Integer arithmetic supports the score calculations, while parity explains why 12 is unavailable.

review.mathematicalCheck: Any two students score at most 24 together, so 13 leaves every rival at most 11. The displayed race patterns feasibly tie at 11. Twelve is unattainable because a zero limits the total to 10, while three nonzero scores have an odd sum. Thirteen is attainable.
